title: Sexton Island: Native Coastal Homeland, Colonial Claims and Municipal Leases
summary: Sexton Island is part of a living Native coastal homeland. Colonial patents, a national seashore boundary and municipal leases record different claims to control; none by itself establishes when Native rights to this island were surrendered.
address_label: Sexton Island, Great South Bay — modern island context
map_geometry_source: Modern Sexton coastline; GNIS964892 point containment and NPS2015 Map3-C cross-check. Not a Native deed or acquisition parcel.
why_this_matters: A government grant, park boundary and lease are not interchangeable. Their differences help explain how control of a Native coastal homeland became organized through colonial and municipal property systems without implying that Native people disappeared.
introduction_title: A Native coast under changing systems of control
introduction_content: Sexton Island is part of a living Native coastal homeland. Colonial patents, a national seashore boundary and municipal leases record different claims to control; none by itself establishes when Native rights to this island were surrendered.
history_title: Colonial claims, a park boundary and municipal leases
history_content:
A small island in a connected Native coast

Sexton Island lies in Great South Bay, west of West Fire Island and north of the ocean barrier. The island and its surrounding waters belong to a connected coastal landscape; the outline here marks the modern island, not an ancient property boundary. Fire Island Draft General Management Plan / Environmental Impact Statement: Map 3-C, Transportation

Native life did not begin with a lease

The National Park Service describes the wider Fire Island coast through the histories of Unkechaug, Secatogue and Shinnecock people, whose seasonal settlements and harvesting long preceded colonial settlement. Continuing Native coastal care, including that of the Unkechaug community at Poospatuck, is part of this history. These regional relationships do not establish a particular village or an island-specific sale on Sexton. Native American Heritage at Fire Island National Seashore

Who claimed the authority to give islands away?

In 1688, Thomas Dongan, the English royal governor of New York, issued William Nicoll a patent for bay islands between an inlet and Nicoll’s lands at the Connetquot River. The later Nicoll v. Trustees opinion examined the patent and the difficulties created by a shifting inlet. A Crown patent asserted colonial authority to grant property. It is not equivalent to a Native agreement naming Sexton Island or proof that Native relationships and rights had ended. Nicoll v. Trustees, 1 Johns. Ch. 166

A park boundary was not a purchase

On September 11, 1964, Congress authorized Fire Island National Seashore. The original statute explicitly included Sexton Island within its described boundary. Being inside that boundary did not, by itself, make every parcel federal property. The law should not be presented as the date Native people sold the island, nor as evidence that it was returned to Native jurisdiction. Public Law 88-587: Fire Island National Seashore

Municipal control appears in the lease record

The Town of Islip’s September 17, 2024 discussion agenda sought consent to an assignment and assumption of a Bay Island Lease Agreement on Sexton Island. This documents the town’s role in administering a lease, not the full chain of title to every part of the island. It shows how modern access and occupancy are organized through municipal property rules. An agenda alone does not establish the outcome of the vote. Town Board Discussion Agenda, September 17, 2024

What land return would mean here

Public conservation, a municipal lease and Indigenous authority are different relationships to land. Reading this coast through Native continuance asks who makes decisions about access, harvesting and care, rather than treating its history as complete when a government boundary was drawn. The island-specific Native conveyance and the intervening title chain remain unestablished in the sources linked here. Native American Heritage at Fire Island National Seashore
